prompt: What is the key architectural difference in how React Native and Flutter actually get pixels onto the screen?
choices: React Native renders using real native platform widgets via a bridge/JSI; Flutter draws every pixel itself with its own rendering engine instead of using native widgets.
React Native and Flutter both embed a full web browser to render their UI, just like Electron.
Flutter uses real native platform widgets while React Native draws its own pixels with a custom engine.
Both React Native and Flutter compile down to Swift and Kotlin source code before they run.

prompt: In the Electron example, what is main.js actually responsible for?
choices: Defining the counter button's click handler directly using JSX syntax
Creating a native OS window (via Node.js) and loading an HTML file into it
Compiling the HTML/CSS into native Swift machine code
Parsing Dart widgets into native Android View objects

prompt: Which statement best describes the real similarity between SwiftUI's @State and React's useState?
choices: They're identical because SwiftUI is React compiled to Swift under the hood.
Both let a variable's change automatically trigger the framework to re-render the UI that depends on it, following a declarative 'UI as a function of state' pattern.
They have nothing meaningful in common since one targets mobile and one targets web.
@State executes on the GPU directly while useState only ever runs on the CPU.

prompt: Why does a web page's JavaScript typically run via an interpreter/JIT compiler at runtime, while a SwiftUI app's Swift code is compiled ahead of time?
choices: Because JavaScript cannot be compiled under any circumstances.

Because a web page's code is downloaded and must run immediately in an unknown browser environment the moment the user visits, while a native app is built and compiled for a known OS/CPU target before distribution.
Because Swift runs slower than JavaScript, so it must be compiled to compensate.
There's no real difference; both are always compiled in the exact same way before execution.

prompt: Which statement about Flutter's rendering is true?
choices: Flutter calls out to native UIKit/Android View widgets for every button and label, the same way React Native does.
Flutter uses its own graphics engine to draw every widget itself, pixel by pixel, instead of using the platform's native UI components.
Flutter widgets are rendered entirely inside an embedded WebView/Chromium instance, like Electron.
Flutter only ever runs in interpreted mode and never compiles to native machine code.

prompt: What makes Electron fundamentally different from React Native and Flutter, even though all three are often called 'cross-platform'?
choices: Electron apps cannot run on Windows machines.

Electron renders its UI using an embedded full browser engine (Chromium) with plain DOM/CSS -- the same rendering model as an ordinary web page -- rather than native widgets or a custom pixel-painting engine.
Electron apps can only be built for mobile phones, not desktops.
Electron ahead-of-time compiles its JavaScript into native ARM machine code the way Flutter's release builds compile Dart.

prompt: In the Jetpack Compose snippet, what does remember { mutableStateOf(0) } correspond to conceptually in the React Native snippet's useState(0)?
choices: Nothing -- the two solve entirely unrelated problems.
Both create a piece of state the framework tracks, so that when it changes, the UI function re-runs (recomposes/re-renders) to reflect the new value.
remember performs a network request while useState only applies visual styling.
mutableStateOf compiles the UI ahead of time into native machine code while useState never does.

prompt: Which statement correctly describes how the 'same' counter button literally executes at runtime in SwiftUI versus Electron?
choices: A SwiftUI counter's button-tap handler runs as compiled native machine code; an Electron counter's button-tap handler runs as JavaScript interpreted/JIT-compiled by Chromium's engine.
Both run identically because all five examples in this lesson share the same underlying JavaScript engine.
SwiftUI code and Electron code both execute inside a sandboxed mobile browser.
Electron's button handler is compiled ahead of time into Swift bytecode before the app runs.
